HEALTHY VS AGED / EXPLICIT ASSUMPTIONS

Same network. Different ways to resist tension.

0–12% of the initial fiber chord; changes actual resting geometry.

0–10× junction rotational restraint; J = setting × 0.0001. Not bond density.

Sliders calculate a fresh 0–4% tension response after a short pause. Calculation runs in your browser and may take tens of seconds. During calculation the dimmed view shows the previous accepted result. Only completed results that pass every force check replace it. Preset buttons always restore the original assumptions.

Hypothetical scenarios, not measured age groups. “Crosslinking” is represented by resistance to relative fiber rotation at existing junctions; no chemical bonds are counted. Lower crimp and 5× restraint are chosen demonstration inputs. They do not imply that all aged tendons are stiffer or share load less evenly.

Exact preset values, evidence and limits

Crimp amplitude / initial fiber chord: 0.08 healthy → 0.04 aged. Junction cosine-spring energy coefficient: 0.0001 → 0.0005 in normalized units. Both are uncalibrated. The crimp-only and restraint-only controls change one input each.

The four scenarios use identical dispersed junction coordinates, 95% candidate retention, 12 neighbor candidates, seed 17 and material budget 192. Fiber axial multiplier 1 and bending rigidity 0.0001 stay fixed. Area adjusts with contour length to preserve the budget. Junction positions are shared in all cases; this model has no inter-fiber sliding, rupture or fatigue.

Human patellar tendon study: older men had more measured crosslinks without a significant age difference in tendon mechanics. Human tendon glucosepane study: age-associated chemical and structural changes do not determine these spring values.

Mouse tendon crimp study: age effects depend on tendon type and loading. These sources motivate mechanisms, not the chosen numbers. No adult human biceps age calibration or claim about biological health, strength or injury risk is made.

What is calculated, and what is illustrative?

This is a synthetic periodic rod network with 16 junctions, four segments per fiber, fixed seed 17, architecture-sweep crimp amplitude 8%, bending rigidity 0.0001, and matched nominal material budget 192. Five load steps span 0–4% constrained x tension. The curved rods include axial stretching, preferred-angle bending and a regularized twist penalty. The initial sparse screen is retained in the source archive; some of those cases were numerically too weak to rank.

Ranking requires completion, all force checks passing, positive endpoint stress, and peak axial force at least 20 times the force stopping tolerance. The added force-resolution gate is a demo screening rule, not experimental validation. Evenness is (Σ peak |N|)² / (number of fibers × Σ peak |N|²). It measures axial force participation, not tissue stress uniformity or biological quality. Stiffness here is endpoint secant stress/strain, not a full tensor or failure strength.

The tubes smooth the calculated chain points for display. Intermediate animation frames interpolate saved equilibria; magnification exaggerates displacement only. These are neither extra equilibria nor molecular trajectories. Playback retraces an elastic path and does not model hysteresis. Healthy/aged labels denote hypothetical mechanical scenarios, not chemical-specific age predictions. No glycosylation, rupture, sliding or calibrated human-tendon prediction is claimed. Chain-resolution convergence remains open.
